title: Unless a grain of wheat falls (John 12:12–26)
hook: a seed must fall into the earth and die to bear much fruit

segments.voice: Yesterday, nard poured on Jesus's feet in Bethany, and a house full of its scent. Your line was the house was filled.

The next day, the city is packed for Passover, and word spreads that Jesus is coming. A great crowd goes out to meet him. John tells us what they carried: "Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord." Hosanna is a Hebrew cry: save us, now. Jesus finds a young donkey and rides in on it. The leaders watch and say: "behold, the world is gone after him." And then, as if to prove them right, some Greeks arrive.

These Greeks are pilgrims, outsiders come to worship at the feast. They go to Philip and ask politely: "Sir, we would see Jesus." Philip tells Andrew, and together they tell Jesus. Instead of bring them in, he says the hour has come, and talks about a seed. "Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." Corn, in the King James Bible, means any grain: here, a single grain of wheat. Kept in a jar, it stays a grain forever: safe, whole, and alone. Planted in the dark, it breaks open, stops being a seed, and becomes a stalk heavy with grain. Jesus is talking about his own death. The Greeks want to see him, and his answer is: the world will see me through my dying. One grain becomes a harvest. Then, for anyone who follows him: "He that loveth his life shall lose it." Not a call to despise life, but to let go of clutching it. Dostoevsky put it at the front of The Brothers Karamazov, as the epigraph for the whole book. Farmers know it without any book: you can't eat your seed grain and have a harvest too. Christians often read these words at funerals, and whenever something has to end so something else can begin.
screen: `A GRAIN IN A JAR STAYS ALONE.`
then, large: `EXCEPT A CORN OF WHEAT FALL.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've been holding too tightly, an old plan that isn't working, a grudge, a version of yourself you've outgrown, a role, a possession, a need to be right, and hold it like a seed in your palm, noticing how hard you grip. Then imagine opening your hand and letting it fall into the ground; you don't have to know what will grow. If you pray, place it in God's hands; if not, notice what your open hand feels like.
Grain. A single seed of wheat, Jesus says, that must fall into the ground and die before it can bear much fruit.
Your line: unless it dies. One grain, and then a harvest. Six hundred twenty-six days now.

chat.says: Why does Jesus compare himself to a grain of wheat?
options: A kept grain stays alone; one that falls and dies bears much fruit. He meant his death.
A tiny seed grows into a huge tree; he meant his followers would soon be powerful.
Seed must be stored safely; he meant his friends should guard his words unchanged.
chat.meaning: Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone. Jesus was speaking of his own death, and the harvest it would bring.

Hosanna.meaning: a Hebrew cry: save us, now

Philip.meaning: the disciple the Greek pilgrims asked to see Jesus

Andrew.meaning: the disciple Philip told, before they went to Jesus together

Dostoevsky.meaning: the novelist who put this verse at the front of a book

notes: Hosanna from Hebrew hoshi'a na, 'save, please/now' (Psalm 118:25). Confirm.
'Only John tells us what they carried': palms specified only in John (Matthew/Mark: branches; Luke: none). Confirm.
The Greeks (Hellenes) are often read as Gentile God-fearers; the script says 'outsiders'. Confirm.
Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov (1880) carries John 12:24 as epigraph. Confirm.
Philip's Greek name and Bethsaida origin (12:21); confirm 'has a Greek name'.
